content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, the winepress functions primarily as a symbol of divine wrath and eschatological judgment: the crushing of grapes and the flow of red juice picture God (or the Messiah) trampling the wicked, whose blood flows out like wine. The image is treated as one of the Bible's most vivid pictures of God's final judgment on the nations.","primary_basis":["Isaiah 63:1-6 ('I have trodden the winepress alone... their blood spattered my garments')","Revelation 14:19-20 ('the great winepress of the wrath of God... blood flowed out of the press')","Revelation 19:15 ('he treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty')","Joel 3:13 ('Come, tread, for the winepress is full... for their wickedness is great')","Lamentations 1:15 ('the Lord has trodden as in a winepress the virgin daughter of Judah')"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Christological/passion reading: the winepress as a figure of Christ's suffering — Christ himself crushed like the grape on the cross, or the solitary treader of Isaiah 63 read as the suffering Redeemer. Prominent in patristic and medieval exegesis (Augustine, medieval 'mystic winepress' iconography) and in some hymnody, though modern critical scholarship treats Isaiah 63 as a judgment text.","basis":["Isaiah 63:3 read typologically of Christ ('I have trodden the winepress alone')","Association with Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36; the name meaning 'oil press,' extended by devotional writers to the pressing/crushing of Christ)","Isaiah 53:5,10 combined with the pressing imagery in devotional tradition"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Abundance, blessing, and covenant prosperity: full winepresses as a sign of God's favor and agricultural blessing; empty or failed presses as a sign of curse or lament.","basis":["Proverbs 3:10 ('your vats will overflow with new wine')","Joel 2:24 ('the vats shall overflow with wine and oil')","Deuteronomy 15:14; 16:13 (winepress in contexts of provision and festal joy)","Haggai 2:16 and Isaiah 16:10 (failed presses as judgment/lament, the negative counterpart)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The winepress in the vineyard parables as part of God's careful provision for Israel/the church — an element of the vineyard God prepares, with Israel's failure to produce fruit leading to judgment; the press itself is incidental furniture rather than the central symbol.","basis":["Isaiah 5:1-2 (God hews out a wine vat in his vineyard)","Matthew 21:33 / Mark 12:1 (parable of the tenants: the owner 'dug a winepress')"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Oppression, fear, or concealment in narrative settings — e.g., Gideon threshing wheat in a winepress to hide from Midian, sometimes moralized as living under oppression or acting in fear; occasionally the treading of the press is used for toil and exploitation.","basis":["Judges 6:11 (Gideon threshing wheat in the winepress)","Job 24:11 (the oppressed 'tread the winepresses, but suffer thirst')","Nehemiah 13:15 (treading winepresses on the Sabbath)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Allegorical readings of the Psalm titles 'according to the Gittith' (possibly 'upon the winepresses'), used by some patristic writers to read Psalms 8, 81, 84 as winepress psalms about the church or the passion.","basis":["Superscriptions of Psalms 8, 81, 84 (LXX 'for the winepresses'), allegorized by Augustine and others"],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is a clearly recognizable consensus: across commentaries, dictionaries of biblical imagery, and popular teaching, the winepress is above all the image of God's wrath trodden out in judgment (Isaiah 63; Joel 3; Revelation 14 and 19). The main interpretive divergence concerns Isaiah 63:1-6: historic Christian tradition often read the lone treader as Christ in his passion (giving the winepress a redemptive-suffering sense), while most modern exegesis reads it as the divine warrior executing judgment, with the New Testament (Revelation 19) applying that judgment role to the returning Christ. The 'abundance/blessing' sense is well attested in the literal agricultural texts but is secondary as a symbol. No party disputes that the term carries strong symbolic freight; the debate is over which passages control the symbol, not whether one exists."}
